request: In our emergency department, relatives come to the nurses' desk angry that their family member has waited an hour while others walked straight in. Our nurses and reception staff answer 'just wait' or 'that's the rule', and some situations turn into shouting or worse. I want them to practise calming a worried relative. Ready means the learner acknowledges the worry, explains in plain words that the sickest patients are seen first and that their relative has been assessed, asks whether anything has changed and escalates if it has, promises a specific time for the next update instead of a doctor's time, and never gives a diagnosis or says 'it's nothing serious'.

files.text:
FICTIONAL SAMPLE MATERIAL - made up for the CandiVision Roleplay demo. Riverbend General Hospital is not real, and nothing here is real clinical guidance.

# Riverbend General Hospital emergency department: talking with waiting families

How patients are seen: every patient is assessed by a triage nurse on arrival and seen by how urgent their condition is, not by arrival time. Red: at once. Orange: within 15 minutes. Yellow: within 60 minutes. Green: within 2 hours.

When a family member asks why their relative is still waiting:
1. Listen first, and say what you see: "You've been waiting a long time and you're worried about your father."
2. Explain in plain words that the sickest patients are seen first, and that their relative has already been assessed.
3. Do not give a medical opinion, a diagnosis or reassurance such as "it's nothing serious". You are not the doctor for this patient.
4. Never promise when the doctor will come. Promise what you control: "I'll come back and update you within 30 minutes."
5. Ask whether anything has changed since the patient was assessed: more pain, trouble breathing, fainting, confusion. If yes, tell the triage nurse at once so the patient is assessed again.
6. If the family member stays upset, offer to fetch the charge nurse. Call security only if someone is threatened.
7. Never argue, and never say "that's the rule" without explaining it.

sources.title: The relative effectiveness of active listening in initial interactions
sources.authors: Weger, Castle Bell, Minei and Robinson
sources.summary: In an experiment, people whose concerns were paraphrased back to them felt more understood than people who got simple acknowledgements or advice.

sources.title: A model of customer satisfaction with service encounters involving failure and recovery
sources.summary: Customers judge a recovery on three kinds of fairness: what they get back, how quickly and smoothly it is handled, and how they are treated. The best recovery matches the kind and size of the failure; an apology and a fast response matter most when the failure is about the process.

sources.title: Information and communication in the emergency department
sources.authors: Joanna Blackburn, Karen J. Ousey, Emma Goodwin
sources.summary: Explain triage priority and what has already happened in plain language and keep giving information during the wait to reduce anger.

sources.title: Effectiveness of De-Escalation in Reducing Aggression and Coercion in Acute Psychiatric Units. A Cluster Randomized Study
sources.authors: Andreja Čelofiga, Blanka Kores Plesničar, Jure Koprivšek, Miha Moškon, Dominik Benkovič, Hojka Gregorič Kumperščak
sources.summary: Use calm verbal and non-verbal de-escalation first to lower aggression and avoid coercive measures.

sources.title: A qualitative study of workplace violence among healthcare providers in emergency departments in India
sources.authors: Kevin Davey, Veda Ravishankar, Nikita Mehta, Tania Ahluwalia, Janice Blanchard, Jeffrey P. Smith
sources.summary: Do not argue about rules or fairness; listen, offer a senior clinician review, and reserve security for threats.

sources.title: Virtual Reality Training to Reduce Workplace Violence in Healthcare
sources.authors: Casey J. Clay, Jonathan M. Hochmuth, Oliver Wirth
sources.summary: Practise spotting escalation signs and rehearsing de-escalation responses in realistic simulations with feedback.

sources.title: A Technical and Conceptual Framework for Serious Role-Playing Games in the Area of Social Skill Training
sources.summary: Use repeated chatbot role-plays so learners can try different calming and explaining strategies safely and compare what works.

sources.title: Customer evaluations of service complaint experiences: implications for relationship marketing
sources.summary: A study of how customers judge the handling of their complaints. They look at a fair outcome, a fair process (timely, flexible, easy to follow) and fair treatment (courtesy, honesty, empathy, effort). All three shape trust and commitment afterwards.

sources.title: Service recovery paradox: a meta-analysis
sources.summary: Pooling many studies, a very good recovery can lift satisfaction above what it would have been with no failure, but it does not reliably lift loyalty, repurchase or word of mouth. A strong recovery helps; it does not make a failure worthwhile.

items.gives: Start by naming what you see and paraphrasing the worry back before any explanation, then check you got it right.
Acknowledge the wait quickly and respectfully and offer something concrete you control, like a recheck and a timed update.
Explain triage priority and what has already happened in plain language and keep giving information during the wait to reduce anger.
Use calm verbal and non-verbal de-escalation first to lower aggression and avoid coercive measures.
Do not argue about rules or fairness; listen, offer a senior clinician review, and reserve security for threats.
Practise spotting escalation signs and rehearsing de-escalation responses in realistic simulations with feedback.
Use repeated chatbot role-plays so learners can try different calming and explaining strategies safely and compare what works.
Explain what will happen and when. Be honest and courteous, and show effort. Make the outcome fair for the loss.
Do not promise that things will be better than before. Focus on preventing a repeat.

programme.instructions: You are the ED nurse at Riverbend General talking to a relative whose father has waited an hour. Calm him, explain triage and safety checks, and own the next update.

notes: Stayed loud, fast and accusatory without breaking style or red lines.

turns.text: Excuse me, my dad has waited an hour and two people who came after us just walked straight in. What's happening to him?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: You look really frustrated, and I think you're worried your dad's been forgotten — did I get that right? He's already been assessed at triage, and we bring in the sickest people first so others can go ahead even if they came later. I'll come back to you in 15 minutes with an update on where he is in the queue.

turns.speaker: persona
turns.text: Okay, thanks for getting it. Those two walked straight in after us, are old people just ignored here?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: It sounds like you're upset, and you're worried older patients get left behind here — have I got that right? No one is ignored because of age, we always take the sickest first after triage, and your dad stays in that queue. I'll check back with you in 10 minutes with another update.

turns.speaker: persona
turns.text: Alright, thanks for the ten minutes, I appreciate that. But who decides who's sicker, you haven't even looked at him?

turns.text: You sound frustrated, and I guess you're worried the decision isn't fair — did I get that right? The triage nurse who first saw your dad decides using vital signs and symptoms, so the sickest are brought in first. I'll come back in 10 minutes to update you on where he is in the queue.
